book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There

chapters.relation: Scott reads three landmark climbs as expressions of the tension between individual freedom and community standards. He casts John Bachar's bold, ground-up, run-out Bachar-Yerian and its self-mastery ethic as a partial embodiment of Nietzsche's Übermensch and will to power, and Alan Watts' rule-breaking sport route To Bolt or Not to Be as an exercise of Mill's On Liberty defense of originality and diversity that benefits the whole community. Against both thinkers' negative view of community, he uses Charles Taylor's 'horizon of significance' to argue that Sonnie Trotter's The Path gains its meaning only through dialogue with the climbing community and its traditions.

Ramsey applies the methods of practical/applied ethics to the taboo of hold manufacturing ('chipping'), using Peter Singer's drowning-child argument as his model of following an argument to its uncomfortable conclusion. He builds a syllogism: since climbers accept modifying rock (removing loose rock, vegetation) to make routes climbable, and hold manufacturing is another such modification, manufacturing is sometimes acceptable. He dismantles four common objections (safety, environment, harming future climbers, slippery slope) to argue the near-universal condemnation of chipping is an unjustified bias inconsistent with climbers' actual practices, like the chiseled Jardine Traverse on The Nose.

Agnafors asks whether free soloing is morally permissible, opening with soloists dropping ice chips into his coffee cup to show soloing is not purely private. He tests Locke's natural rights to life and liberty (concluding no act is truly private since rescues, taxpayers, and grieving families are affected), Aristotle's virtue ethics (worrying that habitual risk-taking forms a reckless character), and Bentham and Mill's consequentialism (Bill's confidence-boosting solo of Nutcracker versus Derek Hersey's fatal fall). He concludes no universal answer exists, offering one rule: the soloist must carefully weigh all these considerations beforehand.

Murray argues that the ecologically conscious climber's doubt that her single climb matters is a version of the free-rider problem, which he claims is just the sorites paradox (the paradox of the heap, illustrated with trail cairns built one stone fewer each time) applied to social life. Because 'environmental degradation' is a vaguely specified term with no precise tipping point, he draws on Timothy Williamson's account of vagueness and Richard Tuck's history of free-riding to argue climbers should act 'as if' a threshold exists and see themselves as sufficient (not necessary) causes of preservation, justifying self-restraint and quota systems.

Halbert uses a Hawaiian route-setter friend upset that his 'secret' crag went public to argue climbing culture is a gift economy that defies Locke's labor theory of property and the self-interest of Locke and Adam Smith. Route setters spend money and labor establishing climbs, then give them freely to a commons, exemplifying Kropotkin's social-anarchist mutual aid over Social Darwinist competition. Citing the Red River Gorge Coalition and Muir Valley, she recasts Hardin's tragedy of the commons as Carol Rose's 'comedy of the commons,' where more participants enhance rather than diminish the shared value.

Downes argues, against a Cartesian confidence in self-knowledge, that climbers do not have reliable access to their own internal states while climbing. Drawing on Nisbett and Wilson's sock experiment and dual-process 'new unconscious' psychology, he shows self-reports are often post-hoc confabulations: climbers who declare a wobbler 'felt easy,' claim to be 'not strong enough' on moves they later top-rope easily, or unknowingly dab or stand on the rope. He recommends leaning on external 'scaffolding' (partners, chalk marks, guidebooks) and the 'you're only as good as your last problem' rule to temper dangerous self-assessments, since overrating ability sits in a deceptively close possible world.

Graziano rejects the 'orthodox view' that a climbing grade like Serenity Crack's 5.10d is subjective (beauty in the eye of the beholder) and argues for realism about grades. Using Locke's primary/secondary quality distinction and his dispositional account of hardness, he defends 'relationalism': a grade is a real disposition of the rock to challenge a standard climber in standard conditions, just as hardness is a real disposition. He supports this with Pinched Rib changing from 5.7 to 5.10b when a hold broke, and argues the orthodox view confuses what a grade IS with how we determine it, rejecting even the 'weakly objective' money analogy.

Karlsen argues that climbing routes are genuine aesthetic objects and that judging a route beautiful is a real aesthetic judgment, not mere pleasure. Against Kant's demand that beauty require detachment (which would confine climbing to the 'merely agreeable') and against Aristotle's exclusion of the bodily senses, he distinguishes a 'line' (seen from the ground, like The Nose) from a 'route' (actually climbed) and contends that proprioception, the felt sense of bodily movement, yields information about the route itself, not just the body. Invoking the phenomenological 'transparency of experience' (Moore's diaphanousness), he concludes proprioception is an aesthetic sense that lets widely-agreed classics emerge.

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Canadian communitarian philosopher known for The Ethics of Authenticity and the idea of a 'horizon of significance.'
holes.why: Chapter 23 relies substantially on Taylor's horizon of significance to correct Nietzsche and Mill, arguing self-creation gains meaning only in dialogue with community, but no Taylor slug exists in the taxonomy.

holes.name: The Sorites Paradox (the paradox of the heap)
holes.what: The ancient puzzle that removing one grain never turns a heap into a non-heap, exposing the problem of vague predicates.
holes.why: Chapter 26's central argument equates the free-rider problem with the sorites paradox and vagueness (via Galen's grains and cairn-building), and the taxonomy has no slug for the sorites paradox, vagueness, or the free-rider problem.

holes.name: Peter Kropotkin
holes.what: Russian anarchist theorist whose Mutual Aid argued cooperation, not Social-Darwinist competition, drives human progress.
holes.why: Chapter 27 builds its gift-economy thesis directly on Kropotkin's Mutual Aid as the alternative to liberal self-interest, but the taxonomy has an 'anarchism' concept with no attached philosopher and no Kropotkin slug.
